solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Sick of being rained on? (5,3,7)

blocks.note: the surface reads this as fed up with, weary of
the setter means a literal position: beneath the clouds, taking the downpour

annotation.surface: Someone fed up with a run of wet days.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sick of' looks like 'fed up with', but the question mark asks you to take the idiom for being ill at face value: whoever is rained on is literally UNDER THE WEATHER.
annotation.definitionFit: Under the weather is the everyday phrase for slightly unwell.

entries.clue: Starterless meal in Oxford area? (5)

indicatorNotes.Starterless: without its first letter, the meal loses its opening S

annotation.surface: A pared-down dinner somewhere around the university city.
annotation.walkthrough: Oxford is not the city but a lace-up shoe, and the upper is the part of a shoe above the sole; the question mark flags the trick.
annotation.definitionFit: The upper is the top section of a shoe such as an Oxford.

entries.clue: End of third, a pitcher scuppered a steal (4,5)

indicatorNotes.scuppered: a scuppered plan is wrecked, so the letters are wrecked and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A baseball report: in the third inning the pitcher failed to stop a stolen base.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is baseball, where a steal is a runner taking a base; the definition wants the other steal, a bargain. The answer is an adjective phrase standing in for 'a steal' as in 'it was a steal'.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that is a steal is so cheap it is almost free: dirt cheap.
annotation.definitionNote: 'a steal' is a noun phrase; DIRT CHEAP is the adjective used of the same bargain

entries.clue: Thrashing headless fish (4)

indicatorNotes.headless: the fish loses its head, its first letter

annotation.surface: A fish with its head cut off, flapping about.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Thrashing' reads as a dying fish's movement, but it is the noun: a heavy defeat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name a one-sided defeat in a contest.

entries.clue: Rash one with fever possibly gets on nut (7)

indicatorNotes.gets on: in a down clue, the first part sits on top of the second

blocks.note: nut is slang for the head

annotation.surface: A spotty, feverish patient eating a nut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint to go with the fever; it is the adjective for acting without thought.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun for someone who acts in anger before thinking, matching the rash one.

entries.clue: Lacking husband, Wag dated around (7)

indicatorNotes.around: WIT and OUT together go around H

blocks.note: a wag is a joker, a wit

annotation.surface: A footballer's partner, single again, has been seeing plenty of men.
annotation.walkthrough: A WAG is British tabloid shorthand for a footballer's wife or girlfriend, which is why 'Lacking husband' seems to be one phrase; only 'Lacking' defines, and 'husband' joins the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean not having something.

entries.clue: A messy wet area around bit of glazed pottery (9)

indicatorNotes.messy: the letters of WET AREA are in a mess
indicatorNotes.around: the rearranged letters wrap the G

blocks.note: WET AREA rearranged, placed around G

annotation.surface: A damp, untidy spot surrounding a shard of glazed crockery.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Glazed pottery' reads as one phrase, but the definition is 'pottery' alone and 'bit of glazed' supplies a single letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Agateware is pottery veined to look like agate.

entries.clue: Paw warmers male removed for hot pets (5)

indicatorNotes.removed for: the M comes out and H goes in its place

blocks.note: standard abbreviation, the letter taken out
H for hot, as on a tap

annotation.surface: Little warmers for animals' feet, fitted to keep the pets cosy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Paw' is a jokey word for a hand, and 'pets' is not animals but bad moods: to be in a pet is to sulk.
annotation.definitionFit: A pet in the old sense is a fit of pique, the same as a huff.

entries.clue: Firm or infirm; sick or old (4,5)

indicatorNotes.infirm: weak and unsteady, so the letters collapse and rearrange

annotation.surface: A list of patient categories: healthy, frail, ill or elderly.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue pairs opposites, firm and infirm; the second is the anagram signal, so the letters of 'sick or old' are the infirm ones.
annotation.definitionFit: Rock solid means completely firm and dependable.

entries.clue: Hobby a corporate exec picked up (7)

indicatorNotes.picked up: heard, as a radio picks up a signal

blocks.note: a = per (ten pounds a head); a suit is a business executive

annotation.surface: A business type took up a new pastime.
annotation.walkthrough: 'a' does real work: it means per, as in 'twice a day', and PER SUIT said quickly is PURSUIT.
annotation.definitionFit: A pursuit is an activity pursued for pleasure, a hobby.

entries.clue: Key ingredient of jam? (7)

blocks.note: the surface wants a recipe: fruit, sugar, pectin
the jam meant is the kind on a motorway, not in a jar

annotation.surface: A recipe question about what makes jam.
annotation.walkthrough: The kitchen reading wants fruit or sugar; the jam is a traffic jam, whose one essential ingredient is traffic.
annotation.definitionFit: A jam on the roads is made of nothing but cars and lorries; take them away and it vanishes.

entries.clue: Loaded or high (4)

blocks.note: high as in strong-tasting or heavy, like very gamey meat or a heavy sauce

annotation.surface: Two slang words for being drunk or on drugs.
annotation.walkthrough: Both words look like intoxication slang; each is a separate meaning of RICH.
annotation.definitionFit: Loaded means wealthy, and rich food or a rich smell is strong or high.

entries.clue: Evil females sons seemed to revolt (10)

indicatorNotes.to revolt: the letters rise up and overturn their order

annotation.surface: Wicked women watching their sons on the brink of rebellion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolt' is the anagram signal: sons in revolt overturn things, and so do these letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A demoness is a female demon, so demonesses are evil females.

entries.clue: Holy? Not so much if condemned to pit! (7)

indicatorNotes.condemned to: LESS is sentenced to stay inside the pit

blocks.note: less = not so much; goes inside BED

annotation.surface: Anyone damned to the pit of hell is hardly holy.
annotation.walkthrough: The pit suggests hell to go with 'Holy', but it is British slang for a bed.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both describe what is consecrated or sacred.

entries.clue: Left in debt, local’s up about inflation (7,2)

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, the word is read upward, backwards
indicatorNotes.about: the turned word goes around L and OWING

blocks.note: the local is your nearby pub; PUB turned upward

annotation.surface: Someone left owing money, with the regulars at the pub complaining about rising prices.
annotation.walkthrough: In Britain a person's 'local' is their neighbourhood pub. 'Inflation' is not prices here but pumping air into something, as with a balloon.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal sense: filling a balloon or tyre with air is what inflation means.
annotation.definitionNote: BLOWING UP is the gerund, used as a noun just as 'inflation' is

entries.clue: Projectile finally going off by flag officer … duck (9)

indicatorNotes.finally going off: 'going off' means leaving, and 'finally' says it is the last letter that leaves

annotation.surface: A shell exploding near an admiral, who ducks for cover.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Going off' reads as a shell exploding; it is the last letter leaving. 'Duck' sounds like taking cover, but it is the bird.
annotation.definitionFit: The shelduck's male, the sheldrake, is a large duck of coasts and estuaries.

entries.clue: Labour fall behind, a victory snatched (7)

indicatorNotes.snatched: the trailing word grabs A and V and holds them

annotation.surface: An election story: the Labour Party slips in the polls and a win is snatched from it.
annotation.walkthrough: Capital L makes 'Labour' look like the British political party; it is plain hard work.
annotation.definitionFit: An old, literary word for hard, painful work, the same sense as labour.

entries.clue: Grad putting up a mum in capital abroad (9)

indicatorNotes.putting up: in a down clue, A is moved up to the top of MASTER

blocks.note: a graduate may hold a master's, so MASTER; its A moves up to the front
a dam is an animal's mother

annotation.surface: A graduate living abroad in a big city, letting their mother stay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Putting up' looks like giving someone a bed, but it moves A upward within MASTER, from second letter to first.
annotation.definitionFit: Amsterdam is the capital of the Netherlands, abroad from a British view.

entries.clue: Coverage provided by work for abuse (7)

indicatorNotes.provided by: the work comes first, supplying the start

annotation.surface: A news report about workplace mistreatment.
annotation.walkthrough: Blocks are shown in answer order: the work comes before the coverage.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean to treat people cruelly and unjustly.

entries.clue: Soldiers invading Urals worked like a dream (7)

indicatorNotes.invading: RE moves into the other letters
indicatorNotes.worked: the letters of URALS are worked into a new shape

blocks.note: URALS rearranged, then split around RE

annotation.surface: A military invasion of the Ural mountains went perfectly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Worked like a dream' is an idiom for going smoothly; the clue splits it, 'worked' ending the wordplay and 'like a dream' defining.
annotation.definitionFit: Surreal describes something bizarre and dreamlike.

entries.clue: Thrilled police department wins contract (7)

indicatorNotes.wins: the department wins, taking the contract into its hands

blocks.note: initials of Police Department, as in NYPD
a lease is a rental contract; goes inside PD

annotation.surface: A police force delighted to land a lucrative deal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wins' is a container signal here: the department takes the contract in, as a firm wins a deal.
annotation.definitionFit: Pleased and thrilled both mean glad.

entries.clue: Right-granting document one’s put in case (7)

indicatorNotes.put in: I is placed inside the document

blocks.note: a patent grants exclusive rights to an invention

annotation.surface: A legal paper, once signed, filed away in a briefcase.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Case' seems to be a container or a lawsuit, fitting the document; it is a doctor's case, a patient.
annotation.definitionFit: A medical usage: doctors and nurses refer to the people they treat as cases.

entries.clue: Unreasonable? Me? Mediator must be mad! (10)

annotation.surface: A party to a dispute, protesting that the go-between must be crazy to call them unreasonable.
annotation.walkthrough: The punctuation disguises the fodder: 'Me? Mediator' runs together as ten letters to rearrange.
annotation.definitionFit: Immoderate means excessive, beyond what is reasonable.

entries.clue: Exam head of maths goes over in lesson (5)

indicatorNotes.head of: just the first letter of maths
indicatorNotes.goes over: in a down clue, M sits over ORAL

annotation.surface: The head of the maths department inspects an exam during class.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head of maths' passes for a teacher; it gives only its first letter.
annotation.definitionFit: The message a fable teaches is its lesson.

entries.clue: Force beginning to hamper ICE (4)

indicatorNotes.beginning to: only the first letter of hamper

blocks.note: the Met, London's Metropolitan Police force

annotation.surface: A headline about a force starting to obstruct the US immigration agency, ICE.
annotation.walkthrough: The capitals make ICE look like an agency; it is street slang for crystal meth, and capitals never bind a setter.
annotation.definitionFit: Ice is a slang name for crystal methamphetamine.

entries.clue: Man of the match perhaps seen by new winger (5)

blocks.note: the game's star is its hero

annotation.surface: A football report: the star player lines up beside a new winger.
annotation.walkthrough: In football a winger plays on the flank; here it is anything with wings, a bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A heron is a winged bird, hence a winger.

entries.clue: Ex-smoker initially found using joints intoxicating (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letter of each following word

blocks.note: first letters of Found Using Joints Intoxicating

annotation.surface: A reformed smoker discovers cannabis is still intoxicating.
annotation.walkthrough: The ex-smoker is not a person but a volcano: Mount Fuji last erupted in 1707.
annotation.definitionFit: Mount Fuji is a volcano that no longer smokes.

entries.clue: Repair shop bishop opened for cobblers (7)

indicatorNotes.opened: the garage is opened to let B in

annotation.surface: A bishop inaugurating a workshop for shoe-menders.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cobblers' is British slang for nonsense, not shoe-menders to go with the repair shop.
annotation.definitionFit: Cobblers and garbage both mean rubbish talk.

entries.clue: City you mostly love in a state (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: most of the word, its last letter dropped

blocks.note: EC is the postcode of the City of London

annotation.surface: A lover declaring affection while in a flustered state.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In a state' reads as being agitated; 'a state' is a country.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the South American republic is one country, or state.

entries.clue: Old cat going cheap at a million (12,3)

indicatorNotes.going: the letters are on the move

annotation.surface: An elderly pedigree cat up for sale, a bargain at a million.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cat' is jazz slang for a man, not a pet; the 'old' one is truly ancient, from the Stone Age.
annotation.definitionFit: Palaeolithic man lived in the Old Stone Age, an old guy indeed.
